topic.title: Factorising ax² + bx + c and more complex expressions (grouping, two variables)
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: A 2- to 3-mark Factorise early (Summer 2025 Q10, Summer 2026 Q14) and a 3-mark Factorise fully in the last third (Summer 2023 Q19, Summer 2024 Q18(a), November 2025 Q22(a), Summer 2026 Q17), the latter often carrying a 3-mark Hence simplify. The same skill also decides the simplify-an-algebraic-fraction questions in M4 and M8.
mustMemorise: Common factor first, numbers and letters together
For ax² + bx + c, find a pair with product ac and sum b; split the middle term and group
Choose the sign of the second common factor so the two brackets match
a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b), with a and b allowed to be fractions or products of letters
Factorise fully means keep going until no bracket factorises: usually a difference of two squares after the common factor
In two variables, every constant carries its second letter: (x + 5y)(x − 3y), not (x + 5)(x − 3)
Check by expanding the middle term only
notOnThisSpec: Completing the square as a factorising or solving method (excluded at M4 by the Teacher Guidance)
The factor theorem or factorising cubics (A level, not GCSE)
Factorising over surds or complex numbers

note.title: Factorising ax² + bx + c and harder expressions
note.subject: maths

mustKnow: Pair with product ac and sum b, then split the middle term and group
Highest common factor includes letters as well as numbers
A perfect square trinomial: a² − 2ab + b² = (a − b)²

notOnThisSpec: Completing the square (excluded at M4 by the Teacher Guidance)
The factor theorem and cubics (A level, not GCSE)

mustBeAbleTo: Factorise ax² + bx + c by splitting the middle term with a pair whose product is ac and whose sum is b
Group four terms in pairs, choosing the sign of the second common factor so the brackets match
Take out the highest common factor first, numbers and letters together
Recognise a difference of two squares after a common factor, and finish the factorisation
Apply a² − b² when a or b is a fraction, such as 9/16 x² − 49
Apply a² − b² when a or b is a product of letters, such as 4x²y² − 9
Factorise a quadratic in two variables, keeping the second letter in both brackets
Recognise a perfect square trinomial such as 4p² − 20pq + 25q²
Use a factorisation in a Hence part: simplify an algebraic fraction, or find a missing side of a rectangle
sheet.howExamined: M4 (calculator, 2 hours, 100 marks). Two appearances. A short Factorise part early on, 2 to 3 marks, often as (a)(i) and (a)(ii) of a question whose later part solves an equation (Summer 2025 Q10, Summer 2026 Q14). Then a 3-mark Factorise fully in the last third, with a common factor containing a letter followed by a difference of two squares (Summer 2023 Q19, Summer 2024 Q18(a), November 2025 Q22(a), Summer 2026 Q17), sometimes followed by a Hence simplify part worth another 3. Schemes read MA1 for the common factor and MA2 for the completed factorisation, or MA1 for the split and A1 for the brackets.
traps: Looking for a pair that multiplies to c instead of ac when there is a number in front of x² (Summer 2024 M4 Q12(b), where wrong factorising produced impossible roots)
Taking out the common factor and stopping, leaving a difference of two squares unfactorised — most candidates in November 2025 M4 Q22
Taking out only part of the common factor: 3 instead of 3a, or 2 instead of 2n
Not recognising a fraction as a perfect square — most candidates scored zero on this case (Summer 2023 M4 Q19)
Dropping the second letter, writing (x + 5)(x − 3) for a quadratic in x and y (Summer 2023 M4 Q19)
Reading a perfect square trinomial as a difference of two squares, so both signs are not negative
Taking out +2 instead of −2 when grouping, so the two brackets do not match and nothing can be factorised
Cancelling single terms in a Hence simplify part instead of whole brackets (November 2025 M4 Q22)

Banking the mark for the common factor and going no further once three letters are in play: the bracket left behind is still a difference of two squares, so square-root each term as it stands, products of letters included (Summer 2024 M4 Q18)

Writing the letter first out of habit, so 25 − w² is factorised as (w + 5)(w − 5) — that is the negative of what you had; keep the two terms in the order the expression gives them (Summer 2025 M4 Q20)

steps.decision: With a number in front of $x^2$, the pair of numbers you need multiplies to $ac$, not to $c$. Writing $ac$ down first is what separates this from the easier $x^2 + bx + c$ case.

options: Because the 6 has to be shared out between the two brackets, and ac keeps track of it
Because ac is always larger than c
Because b is the product of the two numbers
whyMenu.explain: In $(px + m)(qx + n)$ the constant term is $mn$ and the $x^2$ coefficient is $pq$, so the pair that splits the middle term multiplies to $pq \times mn = ac$.

steps.working: Pair with product $-60$ and sum $11$: $15$ and $-4$
steps.decision: Run through the factor pairs of 60 — 1 and 60, 2 and 30, 3 and 20, 4 and 15, 5 and 12, 6 and 10 — and look for a difference of 11, because the product is negative. That is 15 and 4, and the larger takes the sign of $b$.
Split the middle term using that pair. The expression has not changed: $15x - 4x = 11x$.

Factorise the first two terms and the last two separately. The second bracket must come out identical to the first; if it does not, take out a negative common factor instead, as here where $-2$ was used rather than $2$.

options: Because taking out −2 makes the second bracket match the first
Because −4x − 10 cannot be factorised any other way
Because a minus sign must always be taken outside
whyMenu.explain: Taking out $+2$ would give $2(-2x - 5)$, which does not match $(2x + 5)$. The sign of the common factor is chosen to make the brackets agree.

steps.decision: Both terms share $(2x + 5)$, so take it out. Check by expanding the middle: $3x \times 5 = 15x$ and $-2 \times 2x = -4x$, giving $11x$.

steps.working: Highest common factor of $12$ and $27$ is $3$: $3(4x^2 - 9y^2)$
steps.decision: Always look for a common factor first, numbers and letters. Here the letters share nothing, so only the 3 comes out.
The word **fully** means keep going. Inside the bracket is a square minus a square, even though neither term is a bare letter. Rewriting each term as something squared makes it visible.

options: Because a² − b² factorises whatever a and b are
Because 4 and 9 are the only square numbers
Because x and y must have the same power
whyMenu.explain: $a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b)$ holds for any $a$ and $b$, including $2x$, $3y$, a fraction, or a product of letters.

steps.decision: Apply the difference of two squares, keeping the 3 outside. In November 2025 most candidates took the common factor out and stopped there; only the top candidates saw the difference of two squares that was left.
Every term has an $a$, so it comes out first. The bracket is then an ordinary harder quadratic, but in two letters instead of one.

steps.working: $ac = 2 \times 12 = 24$, and a pair with product $24$ and sum $11$: $3$ and $8$
steps.decision: Treat $y$ the way the constant behaves in a one-letter quadratic: the coefficients are 2, 11 and 12, so the method does not change at all.
Split and group. The common factor of the second pair is $4y$, not 4: the letters count too, and this is the step where the second variable is usually dropped.
Take out $(2x + 3y)$. Check the middle by expanding: $x \times 3y = 3xy$ and $4y \times 2x = 8xy$, giving $11xy$, and each term still carries its $a$.

steps.working: No common factor: $\tfrac{9}{16}$ and $49$ share nothing
steps.decision: The first check still happens, and it comes to nothing here. That is worth writing, because it stops you looking for one again later.

A fraction can be a perfect square: $\sqrt{9} = 3$ and $\sqrt{16} = 4$. This is the case Summer 2023 examiners said most candidates scored zero on, simply because they did not look for a square root of a fraction.

options: Because the square root of 9/16 is 3/4, so the term is a perfect square
Because 9/16 must be turned into a decimal first
whyMenu.explain: Square-root the top and the bottom separately: $\sqrt{9/16} = 3/4$. The difference of two squares does not care that $a$ is a fraction.

steps.decision: Apply $a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b)$ with $a = \tfrac{3}{4}x$ and $b = 7$. Expanding the middle gives $-\tfrac{21}{4}x + \tfrac{21}{4}x = 0$, as it must.

parts.workedSolution: The area factorises as $(3x + 1)(x - 5)$, so the other side is $(3x + 1)$ cm. Perimeter $= 2(3x + 1) + 2(x - 5) = 6x + 2 + 2x - 10 = 8x - 8$ cm.

Inside, ac = 4 × 25 = 100 and the sum is −20.
The pair is −10 and −10, so the two brackets are the same.
parts.workedSolution: $4ap^2 - 20apq + 25aq^2 = a(4p^2 - 20pq + 25q^2)$. Inside, $ac = 100$ and the pair is $-10$ and $-10$: $4p^2 - 10pq - 10pq + 25q^2 = 2p(2p - 5q) - 5q(2p - 5q) = (2p - 5q)^2$. So the answer is $a(2p - 5q)^2$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is a difference of two squares, which has no middle term; expanding it gives 4p² − 25q². This expression has −20pq, so both brackets carry the minus.
The a has been lost. It is a factor of all three terms and belongs in the answer.

scheme.for: x² and 16y² recognised as x² and (4y)²

hints: The common factor contains both letters.
2, x and y are in both terms.
x² − 16y² is a difference of two squares.

commonErrors.feedback: The common factor is out and that is the first mark. Factorise fully means keep going until nothing inside the bracket factorises; here a difference of two squares is still waiting.
Only part of the common factor came out; y is in both terms too, so the factor is 2xy.

findTheMistake.stem: Aoibhinn was asked to factorise fully $3ax^2 - 75ay^2$. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The common factor is exactly right, including the $a$. What is left inside the bracket, $x^2 - 25y^2$, is a difference of two squares, and the word **fully** means it has to be factorised too.
findTheMistake.feedback: One of the three marks is safe: taking out 3a, letters included, is the step many candidates miss altogether. The habit that collects the other two is to look at every bracket you write and ask whether it is still factorisable. November 2025 M4 Q22: most took 3a out, and only the top candidates saw the difference of two squares left behind.

findTheMistake.stem: Conor was asked to factorise $6x^2 - 5x - 6$. His working:
studentWorking: Need two numbers with product −6 and sum −5
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The pair was chosen to multiply to $c$, which is the rule only when the coefficient of $x^2$ is 1. Here $a = 6$, so the product needed is $ac = 6 \times (-6) = -36$, with sum $-5$: that is $4$ and $-9$.
findTheMistake.feedback: Notice that the grouping in line 4 was attempted properly — the method is sound, it was fed the wrong pair. Write $ac$ on the page before you hunt for numbers; the moment the two brackets fail to match, that is the signal the pair came from $c$ rather than $ac$. Summer 2024 M4 Q12(b): wrong factorising produced answers of 40 and 6 that could never have solved the equation.

findTheMistake.stem: Sorcha was asked to factorise $\dfrac{4}{25}x^2 - 9$. Her working:
studentWorking: So this is not a difference of two squares
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: A fraction can be a perfect square: square-root the numerator and the denominator separately. $\sqrt{4} = 2$ and $\sqrt{25} = 5$, so $\tfrac{4}{25}x^2 = \left(\tfrac{2}{5}x\right)^2$, and $9 = 3^2$.
correction: a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b) with a = 2x/5 and b = 3
findTheMistake.feedback: Nothing here is careless — it is a gap, and it is a common one: Summer 2023 M4 Q19 reported that most candidates scored zero on the fractional case. Add one line to your checklist: before deciding a difference will not factorise, take the square root of each term, fractions included, top and bottom separately.

prompts.prompt: The four steps for factorising $ax^2 + bx + c$.
prompts.answer: 1 Take out any common factor. 2 Work out $ac$ and find a pair with product $ac$ and sum $b$. 3 Split the middle term with that pair. 4 Group in twos and take out the matching bracket.

prompts.prompt: Why is $ac$, and not $c$, the product you need?
prompts.answer: Because in $(px + m)(qx + n)$ the $x^2$ coefficient is $pq$ and the constant is $mn$, so the pair splitting the middle term multiplies to $pq \times mn = ac$. Using $c$ alone works only when $a = 1$.
$a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b)$, where $a$ and $b$ can be fractions, products of letters, or anything else that squares.

prompts.prompt: What does the word **fully** add to 'factorise'?
prompts.answer: Keep going until nothing inside any bracket factorises. Most often it means the difference of two squares that is left after a common factor comes out.
$\left(\tfrac{3}{4}x + 7\right)\left(\tfrac{3}{4}x - 7\right)$. Square-root the top and the bottom separately: $\sqrt{9/16} = 3/4$.

prompts.prompt: When you group four terms, how do you choose the sign of the second common factor?
prompts.answer: Choose it so the second bracket comes out identical to the first. If $+2$ gives $2(-2x - 5)$, take out $-2$ instead to get $-2(2x + 5)$.

prompts.prompt: Factorise $x^2 + 2xy - 15y^2$. What is easy to lose?
prompts.answer: $(x + 5y)(x - 3y)$. The $y$ in each bracket: without it the $y^2$ term cannot appear when the brackets are expanded.
$(2xy)^2$. A whole product of letters and numbers can be the $a$ in $a^2 - b^2$.

prompts.prompt: How do you check a factorisation in ten seconds?
prompts.answer: Expand the middle term only: multiply the outside pair and the inside pair and add. If that does not give $b$, the pair or the signs are out.

prompts.prompt: What is the highest common factor of $20a^3$ and $45ab^2$?
prompts.answer: $5a$. Take the numbers and the letters together: 5 divides both, and $a$ is in both.

prompts.prompt: When a question says **hence simplify** a fraction, what must you do first?
prompts.answer: Use the factorisation you have just found, factorise the other part of the fraction as well, and then cancel a whole bracket. Cancelling single terms across the fraction earns nothing.

findings.asked: Factorise using the difference of two squares with a fractional coefficient; then factorise an expression in three variables.
findings.wentWrong: Most scored zero on the fractional case. In the second, most took out 'a' and then stopped or could not handle the x and y terms; partial credit for leaving 'a' inside one bracket with the rest right.
findings.rule: After the common factor, look for a squared minus b squared even when a or b is a fraction or a product of letters.

findings.asked: Factorise an expression with three letters using a common factor and the difference of two squares.
findings.wentWrong: A mark for taking 2 out, then trouble with the three letters.
findings.rule: Treat 4x squared y squared as (2xy) squared.

findings.asked: Factorise fully with a common factor of 3a followed by the difference of two squares.
findings.wentWrong: Most took 3a out; only top candidates recognised the remaining difference of two squares.
findings.rule: Factorise 'fully' means keep going until nothing more factorises.

insight.ruleToRemember: Highest common factor first (numbers and letters), then check the bracket for a squared minus b squared, where a and b can be fractions or products of letters.
insight.aStarSignal: Spotting the difference of two squares after a common factor when the terms are fractions or involve three letters.
